title: The Big Bang is a mirror, hiding another universe behind it
subtitle: Cosmic inflation is a figment of scientists' imagination
author: Latham Boyle
introduction: The conventional wisdom among cosmologists is that the universe experienced a period of “inflation,” a brief burst of accelerated expansion, a fraction of a second after the Big Bang. But theoretical physicist Latham Boyle argues that inflation is a figment of cosmologists’ imagination, and that a better theory of the early universe suggests the Big Bang is a cosmic mirror hiding another universe just beyond the beginning of time.
body:
What was the very early universe like, just a short time after the Big Bang? What happened at the Big Bang itself? What was the Big Bang?

Since the universe is expanding, it was denser and hotter in the past. Astronomers can see this directly because any observation of distant galaxies captures them as they were when their light was emitted toward us. For example, when we look at a galaxy one billion light years away, we are seeing how it looked a billion years ago. So looking further out means looking further back in time, when the universe was hotter and denser.

A particularly vivid illustration of this is the cosmic microwave background radiation. Your eyes detect light (electromagnetic waves in the optical frequency range) so the night sky looks dark ­– electromagnetic waves in the microwave frequency range do not register with human vision. But if you could see radiation in the microwave frequency range, the night sky would look bright in all directions. Where does this radiation come from?

When the universe was very young, it was too hot for atoms to form, and instead the universe was a plasma full of separate electrons and protons. As it expanded, it finally became cool enough for these electrons and protons to bind together into neutral hydrogen atoms. This was a few hundred thousand years after the Big Bang, when the temperature of the plasma was several thousand degrees Celsius – comparable to the surface temperature of a star! At this time, the universe went from being opaque to transparent: the photons that were previously rattling around between electrons and protons no longer had anything to bump into, and have been streaming across the universe unimpeded ever since.

So the cosmic microwave background that we see today is actually a kind of cosmic selfie that the universe took of itself when it was very young (a mere few hundred thousand years old, compared to its current age of 14 billion years). This snapshot gives us a detailed and precise picture of the universe at that early time – when it was a thousand times hotter and a billion times denser than it is today.

Prior to a few hundred thousand years after the Big Bang, the universe was opaque, so we cannot see that epoch directly with our telescopes. If we want to “look back” even further, we must use more indirect means.

Can we look back even further? Well, prior to a few hundred thousand years after the Big Bang, the universe was opaque, so we cannot see that epoch directly with our telescopes. If we want to “look back” even further, we must use more indirect means.

Fortunately, we can still use the known laws of physics to trace the universe back even further, and thereby derive observable consequences that can be tested today. In particular, if we trace the universe back to less than one second after the Big Bang, it was too hot for atomic nuclei to form, and instead the universe was full of separate protons and neutrons. Then, between one second and a few minutes after the Big Bang, as the universe expanded and cooled, these protons and neutrons bound together to form the lightest elements in the periodic table (the various isotopes of Hydrogen, Helium and Lithium), in a process called “Big Bang Nucleosynthesis.” By calculating the relative amounts of the various elements (and isotopes) predicted by this picture, and comparing these predictions with observations, cosmologists have obtained convincing evidence that the above picture of the universe is indeed correct all the way back to a fraction of a second after the Big Bang.

When we trace the universe back even further, we encounter an intriguing puzzle. We know that every particle has an anti-particle (a particle with exactly the same mass, but the opposite electric charge). Tracing the universe back to a tiny fraction of a second after the Big Bang, we find that, in contrast to the universe today (which contains almost exclusively particles, with almost no anti-particles), the very early universe was so hot that the number of particles must have been almost equal to the number of anti-particles. But if there had been precisely the same number of particles and anti-particles then, when the universe became cool enough for particles and anti-particles to annihilate, every particle would have found a corresponding anti-particle partner to annihilate with, and we would have been left with a universe filled purely with the radiation left over from their annihilation. This would be a universe with no remaining matter to make interesting things like galaxies, stars, planets and people – in short, a universe very different from the one we see!

Instead, there must have been a slight excess of particles over anti-particles: roughly speaking, for every billion anti-particles in the very early universe, there must have been a billion and *one* particles so that, when the universe became cool enough for them to annihilate, every anti-particle would have found a corresponding particle to annihilate, but one in a billion particles would have been stranded, without an anti-particle to annihilate. These rare, one-in-a-billion remnant particles constitute the remaining matter in the universe today – the stuff that you and I are made of.

(A wonderful introduction to all of these topics is the 1977 book The First Three Minutes by the great physicist Steven Weinberg, who passed away in 2021.)

But why did the primordial universe have this slight (one-in-a-billion) excess of particles over anti-particles? This question was posed and analyzed in 1967 by the brilliant Soviet physicist and dissident Andrei Sakharov who, in 1950, invented the Tokomak (still the leading design for a magnetically confined fusion reactor), and, later in life, won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize. His 1967 analysis led him to realize (among other things) that the total number of “baryons” (protons and neutrons minus anti-protons and anti-neutrons) in the universe can change with time (a fact that we now know to be true, but which was a radical suggestion at the time).

Although we still don’t know for sure the correct answer to Sakharov’s original question, a collection of other experimental and theoretical clues obtained over the intervening decades now point to the most likely answer: In addition to the three types of “left-handed neutrinos” that we have already directly observed in our particle detectors, the standard model seems to contain three other types of “right-handed neutrinos.” (A particle is called “right-handed” or “left-handed” depending on whether its “spin” axis points in the same direction, or in the opposite direction, from its momentum.) Because of the structure of the current laws of physics – the so called “standard model of particle physics” – these right-handed neutrinos turn out to be much more difficult to directly detect than their left-handed counterparts, but a number of indirect lines of evidence now point to their existence. We know that two of these three right-handed neutrinos must be unstable, so that, in the very early universe, they would have decayed into other particles, and their decay can produce the universe’s slight excess of particles over antiparticles, in a process called “leptogenesis”.

If this is the correct answer to Sakharov’s original question, it is still not the end of the story, since it leaves other crucial questions about the early universe unanswered. Due to the enormous subsequent progress in theoretical physics, experimental physics, and observational astronomy and cosmology, cosmologists now know much more about the infant universe than Sakharov did in 1967. And what we have learned is remarkable and striking.

To make a long story short: as we look back closer and closer to the Big Bang, we find that the universe gets simpler and simpler! Indeed, a fraction of a second after the Bang, the universe appears to have been as simple as possible, in every way we have so far been able to check (or have thought to check). This is our central clue about the early universe – and the question is what is it trying to tell us?

The conventional interpretation is that, even further in the past, the universe experienced a period of “inflation” (a brief burst of accelerated expansion, which “ironed out” whatever “mess” preceded it, leading to the simple early state we infer a fraction of a second after the Big Bang).

We have no theoretical or experimental evidence for the hypothetical earlier “mess” which inflation is designed to clean up. I suspect it is just a figment of our imagination.

However, I have come to think this inflationary interpretation is unlikely to be correct. For one thing, we have no theoretical or experimental evidence for the hypothetical earlier “mess” which inflation is designed to clean up. I suspect it is just a figment of our imagination. Moreover, I am bothered by the fact that the basic underlying idea of inflation – that the universe underwent a period of acceleration – turns out to be too flexible and loose: for every particular model of inflation that predicts one thing, there is another published model of inflation that predicts the opposite, so that inflation seems able to explain or predict anything. This doesn’t smell right to me. A good theory is like a key sliding into a lock – you can tell when you have found the correct one because it is rigid, yet clearly fits.

Over the past few years, my collaborator Neil Turok and I have been developing a new theory of the early universe, that we believe provides a better, more rigid (and more predictive) explanation of the simple state that cosmologists observe in the early universe. The key idea in our theory is that the Big Bang is a special kind of mirror – a “CPT mirror.”

Here “C,” “P,” and “T” stand for “charge conjugation” (swapping every particle with its antiparticle), “parity” (reflecting space in an ordinary mirror), and “time reversal” (running everything backward in time). If we perform the operations C, P and T separately, or in pairs, they are not symmetries of the laws of nature, but CPT (the combination of all three operations) is known to be an exact symmetry of the laws of nature. (This means that, if any physical process is allowed by the laws of nature, then the version of that process transformed by CPT is also allowed, and vice versa.) Our theory is based on the idea that the state of our universe as a whole also respects this symmetry, with the Big Bang as the “center” (or more correctly “surface”) of symmetry.

Whereas there is a slight (one in a billion) excess of particles over anti-particles on “our” side of the Big Bang, there is precisely the opposite slight excess of anti-particles over particles in the “mirror universe” on the “other side” of the Big Bang.

One implication of this cosmological picture is that, whereas there is a slight (one in a billion) excess of particles over anti-particles on “our” side of the Big Bang, there is precisely the opposite slight excess of anti-particles over particles in the “mirror universe” on the “other side” of the Big Bang.

We have grown increasingly excited, because this simple and rigid idea seems to explain a surprisingly large number of the observed properties of the early universe. It also makes a number of testable predictions for forthcoming experiments and astronomical observations (for example, the prediction that the lightest neutrino is massless, which will be tested by forthcoming cosmological observations), and if the experiments disagree with these predictions, the theory will be ruled out! Meanwhile, much remains to be understood.

If you are interested in learning about the idea at a more technical level, the best starting point is probably our original short paper “CPT-Symmetric Universe” (Latham Boyle and Neil Turok, Physical Review Letters, 2018).
